overlap.title: Swearing by God’s name differs from Matthew’s prohibition of oaths
overlap.summary: Deuteronomy prescribes swearing by God’s name; Matthew’s Jesus tells his hearers not to swear at all.
overlap.reasoning: The directions differ when read as general rules for the same oath-taking practice. Restricting Matthew to evasive everyday oaths or distinguishing covenant settings may reconcile them, but the broad prohibition does not expressly state those limits.
overlap.scope: This compares the wording. Later religious and legal distinctions need separate evidence; no single harmonization is presented as settled.

overlap.title: An escape story becomes a recurring observance
overlap.summary: Passover instructions connect household ritual, the departure narrative and explanation to future children.
overlap.reasoning: The chapter presents a ritual with an explanation rooted in the narrated rescue. It combines instructions for commemoration with the story those instructions ask later generations to remember.
overlap.scope: A text prescribing a recurring festival does not independently establish when every element of the festival originated, how uniformly it was practiced or the historicity of the departure.

overlap.title: Household Passover instructions and the chosen sanctuary differ
overlap.summary: Exodus describes Passover in houses; Deuteronomy requires sacrifice at the chosen place.
overlap.reasoning: The settings differ: an escape-night household rite and a settlement-era pilgrimage rule. This can explain changed instructions, although Exodus also directs later observance and does not spell out that transition.
overlap.scope: The texts alone do not identify the sanctuary, date centralization or prove historical enforcement. Cooking terminology and the range of permitted animals remain separate questions.

overlap.title: A written law is entrusted for custody and periodic public reading
overlap.summary: The narrative attributes law writing to Moses and directs custody beside the ark and a seven-year public reading.
overlap.reasoning: A narrative attribution to Moses is evidence of the authorship claim made within the book, rather than external verification of the surviving book’s complete composition. The closing narrator’s perspective must be distinguished from the earlier law-writing attribution; this distinction alone does not identify an author, editor or date.
overlap.scope: This does not identify the deposited manuscript, establish its survival or show how regularly the reading occurred.

checks.overlapDecision: Distinct singular/plural G comparison beside the narrator/custody record and the separate burier-identity Q; neither text identifies its burier.
